parole.significato: appended to nouns, adjectives and verbs to form masculine nouns of various meanings;
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-akъ, or from Old East Slavic -акъ (-akŭ).

parole.significato: Used to form adjectives from nouns; -ish, -y.
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *-ьnъ or *-jь.

parole.significato: a being/thing with a given characteristic; often of a colloquial nature: -er
parole.testo: Probably from soft stem + -а́к (-ák).

Of unclear origin. The Russian cognate ахине́я (axinéja) is thought to derive either from dialectal Russian охи́нить (oxínitʹ, “to scold”) (related to хинь (xinʹ, “nonsense”) and хи́нить (xínitʹ, “to abuse”)) or from a seminarian usage of the word афинейский (afinejskij) in the sense of 'falsely lea

From a turkic language (either Turkish makreme or Crimean Tatar maxrama) from Arabic مِقْرَمَة (miqrama, “ornamental fringe, embroidered veil”), from مِقْرَم (miqram, “bedspread”), from قَرَمَ (qarama, “to gnaw”), from Proto-Semitic *q-r-m.
Borrowed from either Czech bašta or Polish baszta, in turn from Italian bastia.

parole.significato: to roam, to rove, to wander
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *blǫkati, from *blǫditi (“to err”) + *-kati. Erich Berneker suggested a possible influence from *lǫkъ (“bow”) / *oblǫkъ (“arch”). Grigory Ilyinsky alternatively hypothesized a metanalysis of Proto-Slavic *ob- + *lǫkati (“to bow, to bend”), meaning "to deviate from the pat
Borrowed from French bore or from German Bor.
Inherited from Proto-Slavic *brudьnъ or possibly borrowed from Polish brudny.
Borrowing from Polish bulwa. Ultimately from Latin bulbus, or from German Bolle.

parole.significato: basilisk, basilisk lizard (tree-dwelling lizard of the genus Basiliscus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle Ukrainian василіскъ (vasylisk), from either Old East Slavic василискъ (vasiliskŭ) or Old Church Slavonic василискъ (vasiliskŭ), from Ancient Greek βασιλίσκος (basilískos). Compare Belarusian васілі́ск (vasilísk), Russian васили́ск (vasilísk).

parole.significato: to own, to possess, to have, to be in possession of
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian владати (vladati), which simultaneously derives from both Old Church Slavonic владати (vladati) and Old Polish władać. Alternatively, a later borrowing from Church Slavonic directly into Ukrainian. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *voldati. Doublet of воло́дати (volódaty).

Inherited from Middle Ukrainian вовъторъкъ (vovtork), овъторъкъ (ovtork), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *vъtorъkъ. Compare Belarusian аўто́рак (awtórak). The word likely received prothetic "о" at some point, though the source of this vowel is unknown. Sometimes alternatively explained as being equiva

parole.significato: to greet, to hail, to salute
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Polish witać, from Proto-Slavic *vitati or arose as a reanalyzation of приві́т (pryvít) "hello, hi" → приві́тати (pryvítaty) → віта́ти (vitáty), in which case came from Proto-Slavic *větъ "agreement". Doublet of вита́ти (vytáty, “soar, dwell”).
Derived via either Polish horyzont or German Horizont from Latin horīzōn, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn).

Borrowed from either German Granit or French granit (“granite”), from Italian granito (“granite”), from granire (“to granulate”), from grano (“grain”), from Latin grānum (“grain”). Compare Russian грани́т (granít).
Borrowed from Polish grubianin (or possibly from Czech hrubián), from German Grobian. Slavic descendants are influenced by гру́бий (hrúbyj) and its cognates.

From Proto-Slavic *duma (“thought, care, council”), Origin disputed. Either from Germanic, possibly Proto-Germanic *dōmaz (“judicial decision, act, thought”), Gothic 𐌳𐍉𐌼𐍃 (dōms, “judgment, act, thought”), 𐌳𐍉𐌼𐌾𐌰𐌽 (dōmjan, “to judge”), 𐌳𐍉𐌼 (dōm, “council, thought”). Also compare modern German -tum, En

Compare Polish zupa, Latvian zupa, Yiddish זופּ (zup). Likely from the Polish, which is itself from German Suppe, from Old French souppe, sope. Itself from either Middle Low German (cf., e.g., sūpen (“to drink; to eat with a spoon”), German saufen (“to drink; to booze”)) or from Late Latin suppa (“s
Borrowed from either German Jod or directly from French iode, from Ancient Greek ἰοειδής (ioeidḗs, “violet”).
Borrowed from either German Kasuistik or French casuistique. Compare Russian казуи́стика (kazuístika), Belarusian казуі́стыка (kazuístyka), Polish kazuistyka.

Uncertain. Possibly from Old East Slavic калига (kaliga, “pilgrim's footwear”), from Byzantine Greek καλίγα (kalíga), from Latin caliga. Alternatively, from Turkic, either the same as Etymology 1 or via some Turkic language from Arabic خَلْق (ḵalq, “people”).
Borrowed from German Karat, or from Italian carato.

Borrowed either from German kategorisch or from French catégorique. Featuring -и́чний (-ýčnyj) ending. Cognate with Russian категори́чный (kategoríčnyj), Belarusian катэгары́чны (kateharýčny), Polish kategoryczny.

parole.significato: department/school/college in a university or institute; chair.
parole.testo: From Middle Ukrainian каѳедра (kafedra), катедра (katedra), ultimately either from Latin cathedra or Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra).

parole.significato: combine, kombinat (an industrial conglomeration in a socialist country, particularly in the former Soviet bloc)
parole.testo: Borrowed from either German Kombinat or French combinat, from Latin combīnātus. Compare Russian комбина́т (kombinát), Belarusian камбіна́т (kambinát), Polish kombinat.

parole.significato: poker (metal rod for adjusting burning logs or coals in a fire)
parole.testo: According to Vasmer, inherited from a Proto-Slavic form, probably with the original sense of “stump, stalk”; compare Russian кочерга́ (kočergá), кучу́рга (kučúrga), Polish koczarga, Belarusian качарга́ (kačarhá), Russian коко́ра (kokóra), коча́н (kočán). Alternatively (but less likely), perhaps a Tu

parole.significato: A brim of a hat, a cap, or other similar headwear.
parole.testo: Borrowed from either Middle High German kritz or Middle Low German kritz through Polish.
From Latin lilia through either Old High German lilja or Middle High German lilje.

Borrowed from English mango, from Portuguese manga, from Malay mangga, from Tamil மாங்காய் (māṅkāy), from மா (mā, “mango species”) + காய் (kāy, “unripe fruit”), or from another Dravidian source with the same basic elements.

Inherited from Old East Slavic мьстьникъ (mĭstĭnikŭ, “avenger”), from Proto-Slavic *mьstьnikъ (“avenger”). By surface analysis, (obsolete) месть (mestʹ, “vengeance”) + -ник (-nyk) or from (rare) ме́сний (mésnyj, “vengeful”) + -ик (-yk). Cognate with Old Church Slavonic мьстьникъ (mĭstĭnikŭ).

Per ESSJa, inherited from Proto-Slavic *mitь, related to Proto-Slavic *mitě, *mitъ, *mimo, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“change”). Alternatively, from earlier меть (metʹ, “throw, sweep, motion”), from мета́ти (metáty).

parole.significato: forget-me-not (any of the flowering plants of the genus Myosotis)
parole.testo: From не (ne, “don't”) + забу́дь (zabúdʹ, “forget”) + -ка (-ka), an all-European calque of Old French ne m'oubliez mie or German Vergissmeinnicht.

Inherited from Old Ruthenian нижъ, нѣжъ, нежъ (niž, něž, než), all of which derive from either Proto-Slavic *ni že or *ne že, or both at the same time. Compare Czech než, Polish niż, Belarusian ніж (niž), (archaic) Russian не́же (néže), (archaic) Bulgarian не́же (néže), Old Church Slavonic неже (než

Borrowed from either German Obelisk or French obélisque, from Latin obeliscus, from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos), from ὀβελός (obelós, “spit, skewer”). Compare Russian обели́ск (obelísk), Belarusian абелі́ск (abjelísk).
Either borrowed from Polish pierwszy or formed in an analogous manner; in either case, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *pьrvъ. Cognates include Belarusian пе́ршы (pjéršy) and Polish pierwszy.

parole.significato: to see off, to see to (accompany someone to a point of departure)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian провадити (provaditi), from Old East Slavic провадити (provaditi), probably from проводити (provoditi) with о → а under the influence of проважати (provažati), or possibly related to Proto-Slavic *vaditi.

From Old Polish *rakovina, ultimately related to Ancient Greek κάρυον (káruon, “nut, shell”) or from Latin arca (“chest, coffer”), via Old East Slavic and Proto-Slavic. Shares roots with Ukrainian ра́к (rák, “crayfish”).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian розумѣ́ти (rozumě́ti), from Old East Slavic розумѣти (rozuměti), from Proto-Slavic *orzuměti. By surface analysis, розум (rozum) + -і́ти (-íty) or alternatively роз- (roz-) + умі́ти (umíty).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian росомаха (rosomaxa), with further etymology unclear. Possibly arising from a taboo metathesis from Proto-Slavic *sormaxa. Alternatively, Kiparsky and Räsänen posited connections with Uralic languages.

parole.significato: shackle, staple (used for locking doors in combination with a hasp)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian ско́бель (skóbelʹ), cognate with or possibly borrowed from Middle Polish skobel. Probably related to скоба́ (skobá) and maybe ско́бель (skóbelʹ) (Etymology 1).

parole.significato: station (e.g. in transportation, or as part of a supply network)
parole.testo: Either from Polish stacja with contamination from стан (stan), or else borrowed from Polish stancja (“lodgings”) with subsequent conflation with Polish stacja. All sources ultimately derive from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂-.
From Old East Slavic стѧгъ (stęgŭ), which was formed either from Old Norse stǫng, or from Proto-Slavic *stěgъ.

parole.significato: to come to one's senses, to recover one's senses, to regain one's senses (to become reasonable, comprehending, or respo…
parole.testo: Melnychuk posits a borrowing from Middle High German schamen (“to feel ashamed”). Alternatively derived from Proto-Slavic *sъ‑xa‑menǫti sę, which Melnychuk finds less convincing. Compare Belarusian схамяну́цца (sxamjanúcca).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; Probably; alternatively
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Ruthenian триво́га, трыво́га (trivóha, tryvóha) (att. in 1574), initially attested as трво́га (trvóha) in 1538, most likely from Old Polish trwoga, of uncertain origin, possibly from *trъvati. Alternatively, considering the Russian sources, ultimately inherited from Proto-Slavic *

Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic оупъвати (upŭvati), either via Old Ruthenian упова́ти, вповати (upováti, vpovati) and Old East Slavic оупъвати (upŭvati) or borrowed later from Church Slavonic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *upъvati.

From Proto-Slavic *xolča, *xolša, *kolša, thought to be borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin calcea. Compare Belarusian кало́ша (kalóša, “trouser/pant leg”), Serbo-Croatian hlȁče pl (“trousers, pants”). Alternatively related to Proto-Slavic *xoliti.
Either borrowed from Russian чува́к (čuvák) or, less likely, from the original Romani source. Compare English chav.

parole.significato: jasper (an opaque, impure variety of quartz, of red, yellow, and other dull colors, breaking conchoidally with a smooth…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic. Melnychuk posits a borrowing from Crimean Tatar [Term?] or from Turkish yeşim.

parole.significato: private business deal, especially a speculative one; gesheft
parole.testo: Borrowed either from German Geschäft or Yiddish געשעפֿט (gesheft). Compare Czech kšeft, Polish geszeft, Romanian gheșeft.
